title: Approach to Abnormal Liver Function Tests (LFTs)
summary: A pattern-based, stepwise evaluation of abnormal liver blood tests emphasizing urgency triage, common etiologies, targeted diagnostics, and initial management. Focus on distinguishing hepatocellular vs cholestatic injury, ruling out life-threatening causes, and avoiding indiscriminate testing while ensuring timely follow-up.
clinicalQuestion: What is an evidence-based, clinically efficient approach to evaluating and managing abnormal liver function tests in adults?

keyMoments.title: Identify emergencies first
keyMoments.body: Red flags (jaundice, coagulopathy, encephalopathy, sepsis, severe RUQ pain) mandate urgent evaluation for acute liver failure, biliary obstruction, or cholangitis [2], [7].

keyMoments.title: Classify the pattern
keyMoments.body: Calculate R ratio: (ALT/ULN) ÷ (ALP/ULN). R ≥5 hepatocellular; R ≤2 cholestatic; 2<R<5 mixed. Pattern directs labs and imaging [3], [4].

keyMoments.title: Repeat and confirm
keyMoments.body: Verify abnormal results, review prior values, and repeat in 2–4 weeks when clinically stable to avoid over-testing and false positives [5], [6].

keyMoments.title: Targeted first-line tests
keyMoments.body: History-driven labs (viral hepatitis, alcohol, metabolic, autoimmune) and ultrasound for cholestasis or steatosis streamline work-up [2], [4], [5].

keyMoments.title: Treat reversible causes
keyMoments.body: Alcohol abstinence, stop culprit drugs/supplements, vaccinate (HAV/HBV), manage NAFLD with weight loss and metabolic control; escalate when high-risk features present [1], [2], [7].

sections.title: Stepwise Approach
sections.blurb: A concise pathway from triage to targeted diagnostics and initial management.

steps.title: 1) Triage for severity and stability
steps.body: Assess for encephalopathy, INR ≥1.5, bilirubin ≥3 mg/dL, rapidly rising aminotransferases, hypotension, or sepsis. **Presence of jaundice + systemic toxicity** raises concern for **acute liver failure** or **ascending cholangitis**; initiate emergent evaluation, resuscitation, and specialty consultation [2], [7].

steps.title: 2) Confirm abnormality and define pattern
steps.body: Repeat AST, ALT, ALP, GGT, bilirubin (total/direct), albumin, INR; review prior results. Determine **R ratio** to classify hepatocellular, cholestatic, or mixed injury. **Pattern recognition** is central to narrowing differential and ordering the right tests [3], [4].

steps.title: 3) Focused history and exam
steps.body: Alcohol use (quantity, pattern), medications and **herbals/supplements**, viral risks (travel, exposures), metabolic syndrome, autoimmune history, pruritus, RUQ pain, heart failure symptoms. Incidental mild elevations are common; context determines urgency and depth of work-up [1], [2].

steps.title: 4) Initial targeted tests
steps.body: Hepatocellular pattern: HAV IgM (if acute), HBsAg, anti-HBc IgM/total, HCV Ab with reflex RNA, acetaminophen level, pregnancy test (when relevant), CK (muscle source), ferritin and transferrin saturation, autoimmune panel (ANA, ASMA, IgG) when persistent. Cholestatic pattern: fractionated bilirubin, GGT, right-upper-quadrant ultrasound for ductal dilation; if dilated or cholangitis suspected, **urgent ERCP** consideration. Mixed pattern: combine approaches [2], [4], [5].

steps.title: 5) Imaging strategy
steps.body: Ultrasound is first-line for suspected biliary disease or steatosis. **No ductal dilation but persistent cholestasis**: consider MRCP for intrahepatic cholestasis or PSC; CT if mass suspected. Use ultrasound in ED to rapidly identify obstruction or steatosis when labs are abnormal [8], [2].

steps.title: 6) Management of common etiologies
steps.body: Alcohol-related: strict abstinence, withdrawal management, nutrition; consider corticosteroids only for severe alcoholic hepatitis (specialist-guided) [7]. NAFLD: **≥7–10% weight loss** target, optimize diabetes, lipids, blood pressure; screen for advanced fibrosis (FIB-4, elastography) [1]. DILI: stop the offending agent; report severe cases; consider N-acetylcysteine for suspected acetaminophen toxicity. Viral hepatitis: treat per guidelines; counsel transmission prevention [2], [4].

steps.title: 7) When to refer or escalate
steps.body: Immediate referral: acute liver failure, cholangitis/obstruction, bilirubin >3 mg/dL with coagulopathy, AST/ALT >1000 U/L, suspected autoimmune hepatitis with jaundice, or uncertain diagnosis with worsening labs. Refer for elastography or hepatology when **persistent elevation >6 months**, **FIB-4 ≥1.3 (≥2.0 if age >65)**, platelets low, or imaging suggests advanced fibrosis [2], [5], [4].

sections.title: Pattern-Based Differential and First Tests
sections.blurb: Use pattern recognition to guide targeted, high-yield diagnostics and avoid unnecessary testing.

cards.title: Hepatocellular (R ≥5)
items: Common: NAFLD, alcohol, viral hepatitis, DILI, ischemic hepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis [2], [4], [1]
Key tests: HBV (HBsAg, anti-HBc), HCV Ab→RNA, HAV IgM (if acute), acetaminophen level, CK, ferritin/TSat, ANA/ASMA/IgG [2], [4]
Consider: Wilson disease (younger patients), hemochromatosis (TSat ≥45%), thyroid disease, celiac if persistent
Imaging: Ultrasound for steatosis, vascular flow if ischemic suspected

cards.title: Cholestatic (R ≤2)
items: Common: Gallstones, malignancy, PSC, PBC, DILI (e.g., cholestatic), sepsis-associated cholestasis [2], [4]
Key tests: Fractionated bilirubin, GGT, antimitochondrial antibody (AMA), ultrasound for ductal dilation; MRCP if nondiagnostic [2]
Urgent: Cholangitis signs → antibiotics + biliary decompression (ERCP) [2]
Consider IgG4 if pancreatobiliary involvement suspected

cards.title: Mixed (2<R<5)
items: Consider: DILI, alcoholic hepatitis, obstructive processes with secondary hepatocellular injury, infiltrative disease [4]
Approach: Combine hepatocellular and cholestatic testing; image early with ultrasound ± MRCP

cards.title: When to repeat vs. pursue immediately
items: Mild asymptomatic elevation (<2× ULN) without red flags → repeat in 2–4 weeks while removing potential offenders [5], [6]
≥3× ULN, symptoms, jaundice, or coagulopathy → full work-up now [2]
Transient rises common with intercurrent illness, strenuous exercise, or muscle injury (check CK) [4]

cards.title: Initial Management Pearls
items: **Stop hepatotoxic agents/supplements**; review OTCs and herbals [2], [4]
**Alcohol abstinence** and withdrawal prevention; provide nutrition in suspected alcoholic hepatitis [7]
**Vaccinate** against HAV/HBV if non-immune and at risk [2]
NAFLD: diet, exercise, weight loss, treat metabolic syndrome; consider noninvasive fibrosis staging [1]

cards.title: Avoid over-testing
items: Use a **tiered, risk-driven** algorithm rather than exhaustive panels initially [5], [6]
Escalate to second-line tests (A1AT phenotype, ceruloplasmin, IgG4, celiac serologies) only when indicated by pattern or persistence [2], [4]

sections.title: ED-Focused Considerations
sections.blurb: Stabilize, rule out time-sensitive disease, and defer nonurgent etiologies.

cards.title: Immediate actions
items: Assess airway, mental status, glucose; check INR, bilirubin, ammonia (context), lactate
Broad-spectrum antibiotics if cholangitis suspected; obtain blood cultures [7], [2]
Bedside RUQ ultrasound for obstruction/stone; early GI for ERCP if indicated [8]
Consider N-acetylcysteine for acetaminophen toxicity or indeterminate acute liver failure [2]

cards.title: ED disposition
items: Admit: ALF, cholangitis, biliary obstruction with cholestasis, severe alcoholic hepatitis, AST/ALT >1000 with systemic illness [7], [2]
Outpatient follow-up: Mild asymptomatic elevations; provide explicit follow-up in 2–4 weeks [5], [6]

sections.title: Documentation and Follow-up
sections.blurb: Close-loop follow-up prevents missed progressive liver disease.

steps.title: Clear plan
steps.body: Document suspected etiology, tests ordered, and repeat timeline. Educate on **alcohol abstinence**, **acetaminophen limits**, and **avoidance of new supplements**.

steps.title: Risk stratify fibrosis
steps.body: Calculate FIB-4 using age, AST, ALT, platelets; **FIB-4 ≥1.3 (≥2.0 if >65)** warrants elastography or hepatology referral in NAFLD or unexplained elevations [1], [5].

steps.title: Reassess persistently abnormal LFTs
steps.body: If abnormal >6 months or worsening, broaden evaluation (autoimmune, metabolic, infiltrative) and consider liver biopsy after noninvasive work-up [2], [4].
